questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests practical CKAD-level validation workflows that go beyond simple deployments, focusing on per-namespace compliance checks, file-based manifests, and secure external reporting.

## Key Concepts

- Per-namespace Deployments with PVC-mounted manifests
- kubeval and conftest for validation
- ConfigMaps for suites and batch sizing
- Secrets for API credentials
- InitContainer tooling setup
- Sidecar TLS rotation
- Readiness/Liveness probes
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting egress

## Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal skeleton for the per-namespace scanner Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ns-baseline-scanner
  namespace: placeholder-namespace
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: ns-baseline-scanner
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ns-baseline-scanner
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:3.17
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq yq && echo ready"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      containers:
      - name: scanner
        image: your-registry/ns-baseline-scanner:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: manifests
          mountPath: /manifests
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      volumes:
      - name: manifests
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: manifests-pvc
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: logs-pvc
      imagePullSecrets:
      - name: reg-creds
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you test and verify the validation pipeline in CI/CD?
- What metrics would you collect to monitor this per-namespace scanner?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical use of NetworkPolicy to enforce zero-trust interactions between microservices and their dependents, a common production pattern.

## Key Concepts
- NetworkPolicy basics: podSelector, ingress/egress, policyTypes
- namespace-scoped rules and label selectors
- Egress to specific app Pods on defined ports
- Validation: simulate allowed and blocked traffic, inspect policy state

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: payment-allow
  namespace: finance
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payment
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: db
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432
  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: cache
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 6379
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt if payment also needs cross-namespace database access?
- What runtime and network-layer observability would you enable to detect policy violations?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question tests practical RBAC auditing skills within the CKAD scope, including multi-namespace governance, secure logging, and egress constraints.

## Key Concepts

- **RBAC objects**: RoleBindings, ClusterRoleBindings, and ServiceAccounts at the namespace level
- **ConfigMap-driven policy**: External policy reference for audit rules
- **Namespace-scoped auditing**: Decentralized audit model vs. cluster-wide approaches
- **Pod lifecycle**: InitContainers for tool installation, readiness/liveness probes for reliability
- **Storage**: PVC-backed logging at /logs
- **Network security**: Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting egress to the audit endpoint

## Trade-offs

- **Pros**: Decentralized scaling, namespace isolation, ConfigMap flexibility for policy updates
- **Cons**: Resource overhead per namespace, potential for policy drift, Secret management complexity, duplicated effort across namespaces

## Minimal YAML Skeleton

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: rbac-policy
data:
  policy.yaml: |-
    allowedBindings:
      - kind: User
        name: admin
    maxServiceAccounts: 10
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: audit-credentials
type: Opaque
stringData:
  bearer-token: <token>
  endpoint: https://audit.example.com/api/v1/digest
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: audit-logs
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: rbac-auditor
  namespace: target-ns
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: rbac-auditor
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: rbac-auditor
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: install-tools
          image: busybox
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - "wget -qO /tools/curl https://curl.se/download && wget -qO /tools/jq https://github.com/jqlang/jq/releases/download/jq-1.7.1/jq-linux64 && chmod +x /tools/*"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tools
              mountPath: /tools
      containers:
        - name: auditor
          image: alpine:latest
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |
              apk add --no-cache curl jq
              while true; do
                kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings,serviceaccounts -o json > /logs/snapshot.json
                curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d @/logs/snapshot.json $ENDPOINT
                sleep 3600
              done
          env:
            - name: TOKEN
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: audit-credentials
                  key: bearer-token
            - name: ENDPOINT
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: audit-credentials
                  key: endpoint
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: audit-logs
        - name: tools
          emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: audit-egress-restrict
  namespace: target-ns
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: rbac-auditor
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: audit-api
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 443
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD patterns: watch resources in a namespace, ConfigMap/Secret usage, PVC-backed logs, InitContainer tooling, readiness/liveness, and a restrictive NetworkPolicy. It exercises multi-resource coordination and security boundaries.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped controllers and watches
- ConfigMap updates and digest semantics
- Secrets for credentials and secure API calls
- InitContainer for tooling installation
- Probes for reliability
- PVC-based logging
- Namespace NetworkPolicy egress controls

## Code Example
```yaml
# minimal skeleton: Deployment (audit-logger), ConfigMap (audit-digest), Secret (audit-token), PVC (audit-logs), NetworkPolicy
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: audit-logger
  namespace: target-ns
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: audit-logger
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: audit-logger
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      containers:
      - name: logger
        image: your-registry/audit-logger:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        env:
        - name: AUDIT_ENDPOINT
          value: "https://audit-portal.example/api/v1/heartbeat"
        - name: AUDIT_TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: audit-token
              key: token
        readinessProbe:
          exec:
            command: ["test", "-f", "/logs/ready"]
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: audit-logs
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you RBAC-scopes affect the watch and updates to the ConfigMap?
- What would you monitor to handle digest collisions or out-of-order heartbeats?
- How would you test this in a CI pipeline?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests per-namespace secret management, rotation workflow, and safe rollouts in CKAD terms. Requires RBAC awareness, InitContainers, and network isolation.

## Key Concepts
- Secret rotation via API and patch
- ConfigMap as state store for rotation timestamps
- Rollout restarts triggered by annotation or config change
- InitContainer for tooling installation
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
# Skeleton: Deployment (agent) in a namespace
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: secret-rotator
  namespace: <ns>
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: installer
        image: curl:latest
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl && mkdir -p /logs"]
      containers:
      - name: rotator
        image: secret-rotator:latest
        env:
        - name: ROTATION_API
          value: https://rotation-api.local/rotate
        - name: API_TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: rotation-token
              key: token
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: logs
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you ensure idempotence of a rotation? 
- What RBAC rules would you apply for the agent? 
- How would you handle API failures or partial rotations?

Why This Is Asked
Tests per-namespace operational hardening: config-driven behavior, rolling restarts, health checks, lifecycle hooks, and disruption budgets in CKAD context.

Key Concepts
- ConfigMap-driven behavior with pod template checksum for rolling restarts
- Tail/log ingestion from a PVC-backed path
- Probes: readiness /healthz, liveness /livez
- Resource requests/limits and lifecycle preStop
- PodDisruptionBudget to guarantee minimum healthy pods

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: log-processor
  namespace: audit
spec:
  replicas: 4
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: "<checksum-from-configmap>"
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: processor
        image: myrepo/log-processor:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log/stream
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "200m"
            memory: "256Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /livez
            port: 8080
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 10"]
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: log-stream-pvc
```

Follow-up Questions
- How would you validate rolling restarts trigger on ConfigMap updates?
- How would you simulate load and verify throughput vs. reliability?
- How would you rollback to a previous ConfigMap or image version?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills around in-cluster tooling, Pod security checks, and non-intrusive governance in a namespace-scoped pattern. It avoids admission webhooks and reinforces RBAC, Secrets, PVCs, InitContainers, and NetworkPolicies.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped Deployment pattern without admission controllers
- SecurityContext defaults: non-root, readOnlyRootFilesystem, runAsUser
- Secret-backed Bearer token for API calls and in-cluster service accounts
- Logs persisted to a PVC; InitContainer for curl/jq
- Readiness/Liveness probes and a strict egress policy via NetworkPolicy

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: compliance-guard
  namespace: your-namespace
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: compliance-guard
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: compliance-guard
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: init-tools
          image: alpine:3.18
          command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache curl jq > /dev/null 2>&1 || true"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
      containers:
        - name: guard
          image: your-registry/compliance-guard:latest
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: compliance-token
          env:
            - name: PORTAL_URL
              value: "http://compliance-portal:8080"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
          command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while true; do ./guard --check-pod-security; sleep 60; done"]
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            runAsUser: 1000
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
        
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8080
      volumes:
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: logs-pvc
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          spreadConstraintLabelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: compliance-guard
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test locally for violations?
- How would you scale this across thousands of namespaces?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests practical canary workflows in vanilla Kubernetes, a common CKAD constraint requiring understanding of traffic splitting without service mesh.

## Key Concepts

- Canary rollout without service mesh using Ingress controllers
- Dual deployments with version-specific labels and selectors
- Ingress-based weighted routing annotations (NGINX/Traefik)
- Service isolation for stable and canary versions
- Rollback strategies using Ingress annotation updates
- Load validation using traffic generation and monitoring

## Implementation Details

The solution provides complete, production-ready manifests showing:
1. **Stable deployment** with higher replica count handling 98% traffic
2. **Canary deployment** with single replica for 2% traffic
3. **Separate services** enabling selective traffic routing
4. **Ingress configuration** with weighted routing using NGINX annotations
5. **Rollback commands** for immediate traffic re-routing
6. **Load validation** using ab, kubectl monitoring, and hit counting

This demonstrates practical CKAD-level knowledge of vanilla Kubernetes canary patterns, proper resource management, and operational validation techniques.

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: daily-archive
  namespace: data-archive
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 1
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: archive-sa
      ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 86400
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          volumes:
            - name: data
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: data-pvc
            - name: archive
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: archive-pvc
          containers:
            - name: archiver
              image: myorg/archive-tool:latest
              imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
              envFrom:
                - configMapRef:
                    name: archive-config
                - secretRef:
                    name: archive-creds
              volumeMounts:
                - name: data
                  mountPath: /data
                - name: archive
                  mountPath: /archive
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "archive --older-than ${ARCHIVE_DAYS} --src /data --dst /archive"]
              resources:
                requests:
                  cpu: "100m"
                  memory: "128Mi"
                limits:
                  cpu: "500m"
                  memory: "512Mi"
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            runAsUser: 1000
```

## Why This Is Asked
This question assesses practical CKAD-level skills in CronJobs, Secrets, ConfigMaps, and job lifecycle management, including verification and rollback strategies.

## Key Concepts
- CronJob and Job resources using the batch/v1 API
- ConfigMap volume mounts for configuration and script files
- Secret injection as environment variables
- CronJob policies: concurrencyPolicy, backoffLimit, and successfulJobsHistoryLimit

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: db-backfill
  namespace: analytics
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  backoffLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: db-backfill
            image: postgres:15-alpine
            env:
            - name: PGHOST
              value: db.analytics.svc.cluster.local
            - name: PGPORT
              value: "5432"
            - name: PGUSER
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: db-creds
                  key: username
            - name: PGPASSWORD
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: db-creds
                  key: password
            command:
            - psql
            - -f
            - /scripts/backfill.sql
            volumeMounts:
            - name: scripts
              mountPath: /scripts
          volumes:
          - name: scripts
            configMap:
              name: backfill-scripts
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
```

## Verification Steps
1. Apply the manifest: `kubectl apply -f db-backfill-cronjob.yaml`
2. Verify creation: `kubectl get cronjob db-backfill -n analytics`
3. Check resource details: `kubectl describe cronjob db-backfill -n analytics`
4. View scheduled jobs: `kubectl get jobs -n analytics --watch`
5. Inspect pod logs: `kubectl logs <pod-name> -n analytics`

## Rollback Steps
1. Immediate: `kubectl delete cronjob db-backfill -n analytics`
2. Restore previous version: `kubectl apply -f db-backfill-cronjob.yaml.backup`
3. Suspend job temporarily: `kubectl patch cronjob db-backfill -n analytics -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}'`

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests practical CKAD skills: autoscaling, robustness, and upgrade safety in real workloads.

## Key Concepts

- Deployment resources and probes
- HorizontalPodAutoscaler (autoscale on CPU)
- PodDisruptionBudget for maintenance safety
- Observability: kubectl top, metrics-server

## Code Example

```yaml
# Deployment patch
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: collector
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: collector
        image: collector:latest
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "200m"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 15
```

```yaml
# HPA
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: collector-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: collector
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 6
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 60
```

```yaml
# PodDisruptionBudget
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: collector-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: collector
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you verify HPA behavior under a synthetic load step?
- What changes if workloads are bursty and you want per-pod CPU caps?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests mounting of ConfigMaps and Secrets, securityContext, health checks, and CPU-based scaling in a realistic, small app.

## Key Concepts
- ConfigMap as files and env
- Secret mounted as files
- SecurityContext (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem)
- Probes (readiness, liveness)
- HorizontalPodAutoscaler on CPU

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-static
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx-static
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:stable-alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        volumeMounts:
        - name: content
          mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
        - name: tls
          mountPath: /etc/tls
          readOnly: true
        env:
        - name: INDEX_FILE
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: app-config
              key: INDEX_FILE
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: content
        configMap:
          name: app-content
      - name: tls
        secret:
          secretName: tls
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you verify that readOnlyRootFilesystem is enforced?
- How would you rotate the TLS secret without restarting pods?
